fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
So I sent messengers to them with this reply: “I am doing a great work and cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it to come down to you?”

— Nehemiah 6:3

Nehemiah is the most personal book in the history of Israel. Most of it is told in the first person by a man who held one of the most trusted posts at the Persian court, the king’s cupbearer, and gave it up to go and rebuild the walls of a ruined city on the edge of the empire. We hear him pray, lose his temper, lie awake planning, and talk back to his enemies. We even hear what he says to God under his breath. No other book of the Old Testament lets us so close to the mind of the man who wrote it.

His name, Nechemyah in Hebrew, means “The LORD comforts”. The book is the story of how that comfort came to a people in disgrace: not in a vision or a miracle, but through prayer, hard work, good organisation, courage under threat and the public reading of God’s word.

The sequel to Ezra

In the Hebrew Bible, Ezra and Nehemiah were a single book, and Nehemiah carries on where Ezra leaves off. The temple had been rebuilt seventy years earlier, and Ezra the scribe, on the usual dating, had come to teach the law some thirteen years before. But Jerusalem itself was still a ruin, its walls broken and its gates burned, and a city without walls in the ancient world was a city without safety, without dignity and, in practice, without many inhabitants.

The book opens in the month of Kislev, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes I, around 445 BC. Nehemiah served as governor of Judah for twelve years (5:14), went back to the king, and later returned for a second term (13:6–7). One of his enemies is known from outside the Bible too: a letter found among papyri from the Jewish community at Elephantine in Egypt, written in 407 BC, mentions the sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria.

The book falls into four parts:

  • The wall rebuilt (chapters 1–7): Nehemiah’s prayer, his request to the king, the building of the wall in fifty-two days in the face of mockery, threats and plots, and the list of the first returning families.
  • The people renewed (chapters 8–10): Ezra reads the law aloud, the people keep the Festival of Booths, confess their sins in a great prayer, and bind themselves by written agreement to keep God’s law.
  • The city filled and dedicated (chapters 11–12): one family in ten moves into Jerusalem, and two great choirs process around the top of the wall in thanksgiving.
  • The reforms of a second term (chapter 13): Nehemiah returns from the king to find the people’s promises already broken, and sets about mending them.

A man who prayed

The book begins with bad news. Nehemiah’s brother Hanani arrives in Susa from Judah, and Nehemiah asks how things are. The answer is grim: “The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates have been burned.” Nehemiah’s response is the first thing we learn about him: “When I heard these words, I sat down and wept.” For some days he mourns and fasts and prays, and the prayer he records is a model of how to pray in a crisis. It begins with who God is:

And I said, “Please, LORD, God of heaven, the great and awesome God, who keeps the covenant and faithful love with those who love him and keep his commandments,

— Nehemiah 1:5

Then it confesses sin, including Nehemiah’s own: “I and my father’s family have sinned.” Then it reminds God of his promise through Moses, that if his scattered people returned to him he would gather them again. Only at the end does it ask for something specific: “Give your servant success today, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man.” And then the book adds one dry line, which explains what “this man” is: “Now I was cupbearer to the king.”

Four months later the moment comes. Nehemiah is serving wine, and the king notices his face: “This can only be sadness of heart.” Nehemiah tells us, “Then I was terribly afraid.” A servant who brought gloom into the king’s presence was taking a risk. But when the king asks, “What is it you want?”, there follows a prayer so brief that the book records only that it happened:

The king said to me, “What is it you want?” So I prayed to the God of heaven, and I said to the king, “If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favor with you, send me to Judah, to the city where my ancestors are buried, so that I can rebuild it.”

— Nehemiah 2:4–5

Between the king’s question and his own answer, Nehemiah prays. Months of fasting have prepared him for a moment that lasts a few seconds, and he has his answer ready: letters for safe passage, timber from the king’s forest, and a date for his return. “And the king granted me these things, because the good hand of my God was on me.” Prayer and planning are never rivals in this book.

A ride by night

When Nehemiah reaches Jerusalem, he tells no one why he has come. After three days he rides out by night with a few men to inspect the walls in the dark, until the rubble is so thick that there is “no room for the animal I was riding to get through.” Only when he knows exactly what the task is does he call the people together:

Then I said to them, “You see the trouble we are in: Jerusalem lies in ruins, and its gates have been burned with fire. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we will no longer be a disgrace.” I told them how the hand of my God had been good to me, and also what the king had said to me. They said, “Let us start building!” So they prepared themselves for this good work.

— Nehemiah 2:17–18

Chapter 3 lists who built which section, gate by gate around the city. Like other lists in Scripture it rewards a slow reading. The high priest and his fellow priests begin at the Sheep Gate. Goldsmiths and perfume makers take their turn with the stones. Shallum, an official over half of Jerusalem, builds “he and his daughters.” Priests repair the wall “each one opposite his own house.” And one group is remembered for the wrong reason: the men of Tekoa worked, “but their nobles would not bow their necks to the work of their masters.” Every name in the list is a person who turned up.

Mockery, threats and a sword at the side

Opposition comes from Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite official and Geshem the Arab, the powers in the neighbouring provinces, who did not want a strong Jerusalem. It begins with mockery. “What are these feeble Jews doing?” Sanballat asks, and Tobiah adds that if a fox climbed on their wall, it would fall down. Here he does not answer them. He prays:

Hear, our God, for we are despised! Turn their insults back on their own heads, and let them be plundered in a land where they are captives. Do not cover their guilt, and do not let their sin be blotted out from your sight, for they have provoked you to anger in front of the builders.

— Nehemiah 4:4–5

It is a hard prayer, in the manner of some of the Psalms, but notice what Nehemiah does with his anger: he hands it to God and goes back to the work. “So we built the wall, and the whole wall was joined together up to half its height, for the people had a mind to work.”

Then come threats of an armed attack, and with them exhaustion and fear among the builders themselves. Nehemiah’s answer joins faith and good sense in a single sentence: “But we prayed to our God and posted a guard day and night.” He arms the people by families, and tells them, “Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome”. From then on, half the men stand guard while half build, and the carriers, the book says, “did the work with one hand and held a weapon in the other.” The man with the ram’s horn stays at Nehemiah’s side, because wherever it sounds, “Our God will fight for us.”

The enemy within

Chapter 5 is a surprise. In the middle of the building, the threat comes not from outside but from among the Jews themselves. In a time of famine and heavy taxes, poor families have mortgaged their fields and sold their children into slavery to wealthier neighbours: “Our bodies are the same as those of our fellow Jews, and our children are just like theirs.”

Nehemiah is furious, and says so. He calls a great assembly and confronts the nobles: “What you are doing is not right.” They agree to return the land and stop charging interest. Then he tells us how he himself lived as governor: for twelve years he refused the food allowance that was his by right, “because I feared God”, and fed a hundred and fifty people at his own table. A wall built by a people who devour one another would not be worth building. Nehemiah closes the chapter with the first of his short, characteristic prayers: “Remember me, my God, for good, for all that I have done for this people.”

Plots, and a wall finished

When the wall is almost done, the enemies change tactics. They invite Nehemiah to a meeting in the plain of Ono, far from the city, and he answers with the sentence that opens this introduction. They send an open letter accusing him of plotting rebellion, and he replies, “You are making it all up in your own mind,” and prays, “But now, O God, strengthen my hands.” A hired prophet urges him to hide in the temple, and he refuses: “Should a man like me run away?” He was not a priest, and to go into the sanctuary would have been both cowardice and sin.

And then, with a simplicity that lets the achievement speak for itself:

So the wall was finished on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty-two days. When all our enemies heard of it, all the nations around us were afraid and lost all their confidence, for they knew that this work had been done with the help of our God.

— Nehemiah 6:15–16

The book of the law

The wall is not the climax of the book. In chapter 8, the people gather in the square by the Water Gate and ask Ezra to bring out the book of the law of Moses. He reads it from early morning until midday, standing on a wooden platform, while the Levites move among the people helping them understand:

They read from the book, from the law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood what was read.

— Nehemiah 8:8

The people weep as they hear it, because they see how far they have fallen short. But this is a festival day, and Nehemiah, Ezra and the Levites tell them to stop mourning:

And he said to them, “Go, eat rich food and drink sweet drinks, and send portions to anyone who has nothing ready. For this day is holy to our Lord. Do not be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your stronghold.”

— Nehemiah 8:10

The next day the leaders study further and find the command to live in booths at the festival of the seventh month. The whole city goes out to cut branches, and booths go up on roofs and in courtyards and squares. The book notes that nothing like it had been done since the days of Joshua. “And there was very great joy.”

A prayer that tells the whole story

Later that month, the people gather again in sackcloth to confess their sins, and the Levites lead a long prayer (9:5–37) that retells the history of Israel from creation to the present: the call of Abraham, the exodus, Sinai, the wilderness, the land, and generation after generation of rebellion and rescue. Its refrain is God’s patience, in words that echo his own description of himself to Moses:

They refused to listen and did not remember the wonders you had done among them. They stiffened their necks and in their rebellion appointed a leader to go back to their slavery. But you are a God who forgives, gracious and full of compassion, slow to become angry and rich in faithful love, and you did not abandon them.

— Nehemiah 9:17

The prayer ends not with a happy resolution but with the truth of their present: “See, we are slaves today, slaves in the very land you gave our ancestors.” Then the people put their promises in writing and seal them. They will not intermarry with the peoples of the land, will keep the Sabbath, and will support the temple with tithes and offerings: “We will not neglect the house of our God.”

Choirs on the wall

Jerusalem is still nearly empty, so the people cast lots for one family in ten to move into the city, and “The people blessed all the men who volunteered to live in Jerusalem.” Then comes the dedication of the wall. Nehemiah sets two great choirs on top of it and sends them in procession in opposite directions, one led by Ezra, until they meet at the house of God. The sound recalls the day the temple foundation was laid in Ezra 3, but this time there is no weeping: “the joy of Jerusalem could be heard far away.”

The last chapter

If the book ended there, it would be a triumph. It does not. In chapter 13 Nehemiah returns from a visit to the king to find that a priest named Eliashib has given Tobiah, the old enemy, a room in the temple courts. The Levites have not been paid and have gone back to their farms. Traders are selling in Jerusalem on the Sabbath. Jews have married women of Ashdod, Ammon and Moab, and half their children cannot speak the language of Judah. The chief promises the people made in chapter 10 have all been broken.

Nehemiah does not take it calmly. He throws Tobiah’s furniture out of the room, shuts the city gates on the Sabbath and threatens the traders who camp outside, and confronts the men who had married foreign wives. In his own words, “I contended with them and cursed them, and I struck some of their men and pulled out their hair.” He reminds them of Solomon: “yet even he was made to sin by foreign wives.” Readers have often been uneasy with this side of Nehemiah, and the book does not ask us to copy his temper. It does ask us to see his grief that the people God had brought home were already drifting away. And its last words are a prayer: “Remember me, my God, for good.”

How to read Nehemiah

Nehemiah is thirteen chapters, and it reads quickly, because so much of it is a man telling his own story. The long lists of names (chapters 3, 7, 10, 11 and 12) can be read more lightly, but do not skip them altogether: they are full of ordinary people who built, signed, moved and sang.

Watch for Nehemiah’s short prayers, scattered through the narrative, often with no warning (2:4; 4:4–5; 5:19; 6:9, 14; 13:14, 22, 29, 31). They show a life lived in constant conversation with God. Watch, too, for the pairing of prayer and action: he prays and posts a guard, prays and asks the king for timber, prays and finishes the wall.

Read chapters 8–10 slowly. They are the heart of the book, and among the most important chapters in the Old Testament for understanding how God’s people after the exile became a people of the book. The pattern they show, God’s word read aloud and explained, followed by tears, joy, confession and commitment, has shaped the worship of synagogue and church ever since.

Nehemiah’s own memoir is generally accepted as the core of the book; it is not certain who joined it to the account of Ezra and the lists, or when, though many think it was done not long after Nehemiah’s time.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices are worth knowing before you begin.

“The joy of the LORD is your stronghold.” Older Bibles render Nehemiah 8:10 “the joy of the LORD is your strength”. The Hebrew word means a place of refuge, a fortress, and this translation renders it so. The picture is of a people sheltered by joy in God’s goodness on the very day the law has made them grieve.

“Faithful love.” The Hebrew hesed, God’s love that keeps faith with his covenant, appears in the opening prayer, where God “keeps the covenant and faithful love with those who love him”, again in the great prayer of chapter 9, and in Nehemiah’s last request to be spared “according to the greatness of your faithful love.”

“The LORD” and “the God of heaven.” God’s personal name is written “the LORD”, following long custom. Nehemiah, who lived at the Persian court, often prays to “the God of heaven”, the title used of Israel’s God in the Persian decrees.

Weights and measures are given in modern equivalents, so the governors before Nehemiah took “about 1 pound of silver” from the people.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Nehemiah 1
fields.body_html:
News of Jerusalem reaches Nehemiah in Susa

The account of Nehemiah son of Hacaliah. In the month of Kislev, in the twentieth year, I was in the citadel of Susa. Hanani, one of my brothers, came with some men from Judah. I asked them about the Jews who had escaped, those who had survived the captivity, and about Jerusalem. They said to me, “The survivors of the captivity who are there in the province are in great trouble and disgrace. The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates have been burned.” When I heard these words, I sat down and wept. For some days I mourned, and I kept fasting and praying before the God of heaven. And I said, “Please, LORD, God of heaven, the great and awesome God, who keeps the covenant and faithful love with those who love him and keep his commandments, let your ear be attentive and your eyes open to hear the prayer of your servant, which I pray before you now, day and night, for the Israelites, your servants. I confess the sins of the Israelites, which we have committed against you. I and my father’s family have sinned. We have acted very wickedly against you. We have not kept the commandments, the statutes and the rulings that you gave to your servant Moses. Please remember the word that you gave to your servant Moses: ‘If you are unfaithful, I will scatter you among the nations. But if you return to me and keep my commandments and obey them, even if your exiles are at the farthest edge of the sky, I will gather them from there and bring them to the place I have chosen as a dwelling for my name.’ They are your servants and your people, whom you redeemed by your great power and your strong hand. Please, Lord, let your ear be attentive to the prayer of your servant and to the prayer of your servants who delight to honor your name. Give your servant success today, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man.” Now I was cupbearer to the king.
fields.summary: In the Persian capital Nehemiah hears that Jerusalem’s wall is broken down. He weeps, fasts and prays, confessing Israel’s sin and asking God to give him favor with the king.

fields.title: Nehemiah 2
fields.body_html:
Nehemiah asks the king to send him to Judah

In the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, when wine was set before him, I picked up the wine and gave it to the king. I had never been sad in his presence before. So the king asked me, “Why do you look so sad? You are not sick. This can only be sadness of heart.” Then I was terribly afraid. I said to the king, “May the king live forever! Why should I not look sad, when the city where my ancestors are buried lies in ruins and its gates have been destroyed by fire?”

The king said to me, “What is it you want?” So I prayed to the God of heaven, and I said to the king, “If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favor with you, send me to Judah, to the city where my ancestors are buried, so that I can rebuild it.” The king, with the queen sitting beside him, asked me, “How long will you be gone, and when will you come back?” So it pleased the king to send me, and I set a time for him. I also said to the king, “If it pleases the king, let me be given letters to the governors of the province Beyond the River, so that they will let me pass through until I reach Judah, and a letter to Asaph, keeper of the king’s forest, so that he will give me timber to make beams for the gates of the fortress by the temple, for the city wall, and for the house I will live in.” And the king granted me these things, because the good hand of my God was on me. So I came to the governors of the province Beyond the River and gave them the king’s letters. The king had also sent army commanders and horsemen with me.

Nehemiah comes to Jerusalem and inspects the walls

When Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite official heard of it, they were greatly displeased that someone had come to seek the welfare of the Israelites. So I came to Jerusalem, and I was there three days. Then I got up during the night, I and a few men with me. I had not told anyone what my God was putting into my heart to do for Jerusalem. There was no animal with me except the one I was riding. I went out by night through the Valley Gate toward the Dragon Spring and the Dung Gate. I inspected the walls of Jerusalem, which had been broken down, and its gates, which had been destroyed by fire. Then I went on to the Fountain Gate and to the King’s Pool, but there was no room for the animal I was riding to get through. So I went up through the valley in the night and inspected the wall. Then I turned back and came in through the Valley Gate, and so I returned. The officials did not know where I had gone or what I was doing. I had not yet told the Jews, the priests, the nobles, the officials or the others who would do the work. Then I said to them, “You see the trouble we are in: Jerusalem lies in ruins, and its gates have been burned with fire. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we will no longer be a disgrace.” I told them how the hand of my God had been good to me, and also what the king had said to me. They said, “Let us start building!” So they prepared themselves for this good work.

But when Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite official and Geshem the Arab heard of it, they mocked us and scorned us. They said, “What is this you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?” I answered them, “The God of heaven will give us success, and we his servants will start building. But you have no share, no right and no memorial in Jerusalem.”
fields.summary: Artaxerxes grants Nehemiah’s request to rebuild Jerusalem. Nehemiah inspects the walls by night, and the people agree to build, though Sanballat and Tobiah mock them.

fields.title: Nehemiah 3
fields.body_html:
The builders of the wall and its gates

Then Eliashib the high priest and his fellow priests set to work and rebuilt the Sheep Gate. They dedicated it and set its doors in place. They built and dedicated the wall as far as the Tower of the Hundred and the Tower of Hananel.

Next to him the men of Jericho built, and next to them Zaccur son of Imri built.

The people of Hassenaah built the Fish Gate. They laid its beams and set up its doors, its bolts and its bars.

Next to them Meremoth son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz, made repairs. Next to him Meshullam son of Berekiah, son of Meshezabel, made repairs. Next to him Zadok son of Baana made repairs.

Next to them the men of Tekoa made repairs, but their nobles would not bow their necks to the work of their masters.

Joiada son of Paseah and Meshullam son of Besodeiah repaired the Jeshanah Gate. They laid its beams and set up its doors, its bolts and its bars.

Next to them Melatiah the Gibeonite and Jadon the Meronothite made repairs. They were men of Gibeon and Mizpah, which were under the authority of the governor of the province Beyond the River.

Next to him Uzziel son of Harhaiah, one of the goldsmiths, made repairs. Next to him Hananiah, one of the perfume makers, made repairs. They restored Jerusalem as far as the Broad Wall.

Next to them Rephaiah son of Hur, official over half the district of Jerusalem, made repairs.

Next to them Jedaiah son of Harumaph made repairs opposite his house, and next to him Hattush son of Hashabneiah made repairs. Malkijah son of Harim and Hasshub son of Pahath-moab repaired another section, and the Tower of the Ovens.

Next to him Shallum son of Hallohesh, official over the other half of the district of Jerusalem, made repairs, he and his daughters.

Hanun and the people of Zanoah repaired the Valley Gate. They rebuilt it and set up its doors, its bolts and its bars. They also repaired about 1,500 feet of the wall, as far as the Dung Gate. Malkijah son of Rechab, official over the district of Beth-haccherem, repaired the Dung Gate. He rebuilt it and set up its doors, its bolts and its bars.

Shallun son of Col-hozeh, official over the district of Mizpah, repaired the Fountain Gate. He rebuilt it, roofed it, and set up its doors, its bolts and its bars. He also repaired the wall of the Pool of Shelah by the king’s garden, as far as the steps that go down from the City of David.

The work along the east side of the city

After him Nehemiah son of Azbuk, official over half the district of Beth-zur, made repairs as far as a point opposite the tombs of David, as far as the man-made pool and the house of the warriors.

After him the Levites made repairs, under Rehum son of Bani. Next to him Hashabiah, official over half the district of Keilah, made repairs for his district.

After him their fellow Levites made repairs, under Bavvai son of Henadad, official over the other half of the district of Keilah.

Next to him Ezer son of Jeshua, official of Mizpah, repaired another section, from a point opposite the way up to the armory, at the Angle.

After him Baruch son of Zaccai eagerly repaired another section, from the Angle as far as the door of the house of Eliashib the high priest.

After him Meremoth son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz, repaired another section, from the door of Eliashib’s house to the end of his house.

After him the priests from the surrounding region made repairs. After them Benjamin and Hasshub made repairs opposite their house, and after them Azariah son of Maaseiah, son of Ananiah, made repairs beside his own house.

After him Binnui son of Henadad repaired another section, from the house of Azariah to the Angle and to the corner. Palal son of Uzai made repairs opposite the Angle and the tower that projects from the upper palace of the king, at the courtyard of the guard. After him Pedaiah son of Parosh made repairs

(the temple servants were living on the Ophel) as far as a point opposite the Water Gate on the east and the projecting tower.

After them the men of Tekoa repaired another section, from a point opposite the great projecting tower as far as the wall of the Ophel. Above the Horse Gate the priests made repairs, each one opposite his own house.

After them Zadok son of Immer made repairs opposite his own house, and after him Shemaiah son of Shecaniah, the keeper of the East Gate, made repairs.

After him Hananiah son of Shelemiah and Hanun, the sixth son of Zalaph, repaired another section. After them Meshullam son of Berekiah made repairs opposite his living quarters.

After him Malkijah, one of the goldsmiths, made repairs as far as the house of the temple servants and the merchants, opposite the Inspection Gate, and as far as the upper room at the corner. Between the upper room at the corner and the Sheep Gate the goldsmiths and the merchants made repairs.
fields.summary: The families of Jerusalem rebuild the wall and its gates section by section.

fields.title: Nehemiah 4
fields.body_html:
Sanballat and Tobiah mock the builders

When Sanballat heard that we were rebuilding the wall, he was furious and very angry, and he mocked the Jews. He spoke in front of his associates and the army of Samaria and said, “What are these feeble Jews doing? Will they restore the wall by themselves? Will they offer sacrifices? Will they finish in a day? Can they bring the stones back to life out of the heaps of rubble, burned as they are?” Tobiah the Ammonite was beside him, and he said, “Even what they are building, if a fox climbed up on it, it would break down their stone wall!”

Hear, our God, for we are despised! Turn their insults back on their own heads, and let them be plundered in a land where they are captives. Do not cover their guilt, and do not let their sin be blotted out from your sight, for they have provoked you to anger in front of the builders.

They plotted together to fight against Jerusalem

So we built the wall, and the whole wall was joined together up to half its height, for the people had a mind to work.

When Sanballat and Tobiah, the Arabs, the Ammonites and the people of Ashdod heard that the repair of Jerusalem’s walls was moving ahead and that the gaps were beginning to be closed, they were furious. They all plotted together to come and fight against Jerusalem and throw it into confusion. But we prayed to our God and posted a guard day and night to protect ourselves from them. Meanwhile the people of Judah were saying, “The strength of the carriers is giving out, and there is so much rubble that we cannot rebuild the wall.” And our enemies said, “They will not know or see a thing until we are right among them, killing them and putting a stop to the work.” The Jews who lived near them came and told us again and again, “From every place you turn, they will come against us.” So I posted people in the lowest places behind the wall, at the exposed points, and I stationed the people clan by clan, with their swords, their spears and their bows. After I had looked things over, I stood up and said to the nobles, the officials and the rest of the people, “Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons and daughters, your wives and your homes.”

The work goes on under guard

When our enemies heard that we knew of their plan and that God had brought it to nothing, we all went back to the wall, each to his own work. From that day on, half of my men did the work while the other half held the spears, shields, bows and armor. The commanders stood behind all the people of Judah who were rebuilding the wall. Those who carried loads did the work with one hand and held a weapon in the other. Each of the builders had his sword strapped to his side as he built, and the man who sounded the ram’s horn stayed beside me. Then I said to the nobles, the officials and the rest of the people, “The work is large and spread out, and we are scattered along the wall, far from one another. Wherever you hear the sound of the ram’s horn, rally to us there. Our God will fight for us.” So we kept at the work, with half the men holding spears, from the first light of dawn until the stars came out. At that time I also told the people, “Let every man and his servant stay the night inside Jerusalem, so that they can serve as guards for us at night and work by day.” Neither I nor my relatives nor my men nor the guards who followed me took off our clothes. Each of us kept his weapon with him, even when going for water.
fields.summary: Enemies mock and plot to attack, and Nehemiah sets guards; the builders work with a weapon in one hand. The wall rises as the people pray and work.

fields.title: Nehemiah 5
fields.body_html:
The outcry of the poor against their own people

Now the common people and their wives raised a great outcry against their fellow Jews. Some were saying, “We and our sons and daughters are many. We must get grain so that we can eat and stay alive.” Others were saying, “We are mortgaging our fields, our vineyards and our houses to get grain during the famine.” Still others said, “We have borrowed money against our fields and vineyards to pay the king’s tax. Our bodies are the same as those of our fellow Jews, and our children are just like theirs. Yet we are forcing our sons and daughters into slavery. Some of our daughters have already been taken as slaves, and we are powerless, because our fields and vineyards now belong to others.” I was very angry when I heard their outcry and these complaints. After thinking it over, I brought charges against the nobles and the officials. I told them, “You are charging your own fellow Jews interest!” Then I called a great assembly to deal with them. I said to them, “As far as we were able, we have bought back our fellow Jews who had been sold to foreigners. And now you are selling your own fellow Jews, only for them to be sold back to us!” They kept silent and could find nothing to say.

I went on, “What you are doing is not right. Should you not live in the fear of our God, so that the nations who are our enemies have no reason to mock us? I myself, my relatives and my men are also lending them money and grain. Let us stop charging this interest! Give back to them this very day their fields, vineyards, olive groves and houses, and the interest you are charging them on the money, grain, new wine and olive oil.” They answered, “We will give it back and demand nothing more from them. We will do exactly as you say.” Then I called the priests and made the nobles and officials take an oath to do what they had promised. I also shook out the fold of my robe and said, “In the same way may God shake out of his house and his property anyone who does not keep this promise. May he be shaken out like this and left with nothing!” The whole assembly said, “Amen,” and praised the LORD. And the people did as they had promised. Moreover, from the day I was appointed to be their governor in the land of Judah, from the twentieth year to the thirty-second year of King Artaxerxes, twelve years in all, neither I nor my relatives ate the food allowance of the governor. The earlier governors before me had laid heavy burdens on the people. They took food and wine from them, as well as about 1 pound of silver. Even their servants lorded it over the people. But I did not act like that, because I feared God. I devoted myself to the work on this wall, and we did not acquire any land. All my men were gathered there for the work. Besides, 150 Jews and officials ate at my table, as well as those who came to us from the surrounding nations. Each day one ox, six choice sheep and some birds were prepared for me, and every ten days a large supply of all kinds of wine. In spite of all this, I never demanded the governor’s food allowance, because the people already carried a heavy burden. Remember me, my God, for good, for all that I have done for this people.
fields.summary: Poor families complain that they must mortgage their fields and sell their children to pay debts. Nehemiah rebukes the nobles, has the debts cancelled, and as governor does not take his allowance.

fields.title: Nehemiah 6
fields.body_html:
Come, let us meet together

Sanballat, Tobiah, Geshem the Arab and the rest of our enemies heard that I had rebuilt the wall and that not one gap was left in it, though by then I had not yet hung the doors in the gates. Sanballat and Geshem sent me a message: “Come, let us meet together at Kephirim in the plain of Ono.” But they were planning to harm me. So I sent messengers to them with this reply: “I am doing a great work and cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it to come down to you?” Four times they sent me the same message, and each time I gave them the same answer.

The fifth time, Sanballat sent his servant to me with the same message, and he had an open letter in his hand. In it was written: “It is reported among the nations, and Geshem confirms it, that you and the Jews are planning to revolt. That is why you are building the wall. According to these reports, you are about to become their king. You have even appointed prophets to announce about you in Jerusalem, ‘There is a king in Judah!’ Now this report will reach the king. So come, let us talk this over together.”

I sent him this reply: “Nothing like what you are saying has happened. You are making it all up in your own mind.” They were all trying to frighten us, thinking, “Their hands will grow too weak for the work, and it will never be finished.” But now, O God, strengthen my hands. One day I went to the house of Shemaiah son of Delaiah, son of Mehetabel, who was confined to his home. He said, “Let us meet in the house of God, inside the temple, and shut the temple doors, because they are coming to kill you. They are coming at night to kill you!” But I said, “Should a man like me run away? And could someone like me go into the temple and live? I will not go in!” Then I realized that God had not sent him. He had spoken this prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him. He had been hired to frighten me into doing this and sinning, so that they could give me a bad name and discredit me.

The wall finished in fifty-two days

Remember, my God, what Tobiah and Sanballat have done, and also Noadiah the prophetess and the rest of the prophets who have been trying to frighten me. So the wall was finished on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty-two days.

When all our enemies heard of it, all the nations around us were afraid and lost all their confidence, for they knew that this work had been done with the help of our God. Also in those days the nobles of Judah were sending many letters to Tobiah, and letters from Tobiah kept coming to them. Many in Judah were bound to him by oath, because he was the son-in-law of Shecaniah son of Arah, and his son Jehohanan had married the daughter of Meshullam son of Berekiah. They kept telling me about his good deeds, and then they reported to him what I said. And Tobiah kept sending letters to frighten me.
fields.summary: Sanballat and his allies try to lure and frighten Nehemiah, but he refuses. The wall is finished in fifty-two days.

fields.title: Nehemiah 7
fields.body_html:
Gates, guards and an empty city

When the wall had been rebuilt and I had set the doors in place, and the gatekeepers, the singers and the Levites had been appointed to their duties, I put my brother Hanani in charge of Jerusalem, together with Hananiah the commander of the citadel, for he was a faithful man who feared God more than most. I said to them, “The gates of Jerusalem must not be opened until the sun is hot, and while the gatekeepers are still on duty, have them shut the doors and bar them. Appoint guards from the people who live in Jerusalem, some at their posts and some in front of their own houses.” The city was spacious and large, but there were few people in it, and the houses had not been rebuilt. Then my God put it into my heart to gather the nobles, the officials and the people to be enrolled by their family lines. I found the genealogical record of those who had come back first, and this is what I found written in it:

The people of the province who came up from captivity

These are the people of the province who came up from the captivity of the exiles whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away, and who returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to their own town. They came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Azariah, Raamiah, Nahamani, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispereth, Bigvai, Nehum and Baanah. The number of the men of the people of Israel:

the descendants of Parosh, 2,172;

the descendants of Shephatiah, 372;

the descendants of Arah, 652;

the descendants of Pahath-moab, of the line of Jeshua and Joab, 2,818;

the descendants of Elam, 1,254;

the descendants of Zattu, 845;

the descendants of Zaccai, 760;

the descendants of Binnui, 648;

the descendants of Bebai, 628;

the descendants of Azgad, 2,322;

the descendants of Adonikam, 667;

the descendants of Bigvai, 2,067;

the descendants of Adin, 655;

the descendants of Ater, that is, of Hezekiah, ninety-eight;

the descendants of Hashum, 328;

the descendants of Bezai, 324;

the descendants of Hariph, 112;

The men counted by their towns

the people of Gibeon, ninety-five;

the men of Bethlehem and Netophah, 188;

the men of Anathoth, 128;

the men of Beth-azmaveth, forty-two;

the men of Kiriath-jearim, Kephirah and Beeroth, 743;

the men of Ramah and Geba, 621;

the men of Micmash, 122;

the men of Bethel and Ai, 123;

the men of the other Nebo, fifty-two;

the descendants of the other Elam, 1,254;

the descendants of Harim, 320;

the people of Jericho, 345;

the people of Lod, Hadid and Ono, 721;

the people of Senaah, 3,930.

Priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants

The priests: the descendants of Jedaiah, of the house of Jeshua, 973;

the descendants of Immer, 1,052;

the descendants of Pashhur, 1,247;

the descendants of Harim, 1,017.

The Levites: the descendants of Jeshua and Kadmiel, of the line of Hodevah, seventy-four.

The singers: the descendants of Asaph, 148.

The gatekeepers: the descendants of Shallum, the descendants of Ater, the descendants of Talmon, the descendants of Akkub, the descendants of Hatita, the descendants of Shobai, 138.

The temple servants: the descendants of Ziha, the descendants of Hasupha, the descendants of Tabbaoth, the descendants of Keros, the descendants of Sia, the descendants of Padon, the descendants of Lebanah, the descendants of Hagabah, the descendants of Shalmai, the descendants of Hanan, the descendants of Giddel, the descendants of Gahar, the descendants of Reaiah, the descendants of Rezin, the descendants of Nekoda, the descendants of Gazzam, the descendants of Uzzah, the descendants of Paseah, the descendants of Besai, the descendants of Meunim, the descendants of Nephishesim, the descendants of Bakbuk, the descendants of Hakupha, the descendants of Harhur, the descendants of Bazlith, the descendants of Mehida, the descendants of Harsha, the descendants of Barkos, the descendants of Sisera, the descendants of Temah, the descendants of Neziah, the descendants of Hatipha. The descendants of Solomon’s servants: the descendants of Sotai, the descendants of Sophereth, the descendants of Perida, the descendants of Jaala, the descendants of Darkon, the descendants of Giddel, the descendants of Shephatiah, the descendants of Hattil, the descendants of Pokereth-hazzebaim, the descendants of Amon. All the temple servants and the descendants of Solomon’s servants: 392.

Those who could not prove their descent

These are the ones who came up from Tel Melah, Tel Harsha, Kerub, Addon and Immer, but they could not show their family or their descent, whether they were from Israel: the descendants of Delaiah, the descendants of Tobiah, the descendants of Nekoda, 642.

And of the priests: the descendants of Hobaiah, the descendants of Hakkoz, the descendants of Barzillai, who had married one of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite and was called by their name. These searched for their record among those enrolled by genealogy, but it could not be found, so they were excluded from the priesthood as unclean. The governor told them that they were not to eat any of the most holy food until there was a priest to consult the Urim and Thummim. The whole assembly together numbered 42,360, not counting their male and female slaves, who numbered 7,337. They also had 245 male and female singers.

There were 435 camels and 6,720 donkeys. Some of the heads of families gave to the work. The governor gave to the treasury 1,000 gold darics, fifty bowls and 530 garments for priests. Some of the heads of families gave to the treasury for the work 20,000 gold darics and about 2,750 pounds of silver. What the rest of the people gave was 20,000 gold darics, about 2,500 pounds of silver and sixty-seven garments for priests.

So the priests, the Levites, the gatekeepers, the singers, some of the people, the temple servants and all Israel settled in their towns. When the seventh month came, the Israelites were in their towns.
fields.summary: Nehemiah appoints gatekeepers and leaders. The list of the exiles who first returned is given again.

fields.title: Nehemiah 8
fields.body_html:
Ezra reads the book of the law

All the people gathered together as one to the square in front of the Water Gate. They asked Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses, which the LORD had commanded for Israel. So Ezra the priest brought the law before the assembly, men and women and all who could understand what they heard. It was the first day of the seventh month. He read from it, facing the square in front of the Water Gate, from early morning until midday, before the men and women and those who could understand. And all the people listened closely to the book of the law. Ezra the scribe stood on a wooden platform that had been built for the occasion. Beside him on his right stood Mattithiah, Shema, Anaiah, Uriah, Hilkiah and Maaseiah, and on his left Pedaiah, Mishael, Malkijah, Hashum, Hashbaddanah, Zechariah and Meshullam.

Ezra opened the book in the sight of all the people, since he stood above them all. And as he opened it, all the people stood up. Ezra blessed the LORD, the great God, and all the people lifted up their hands and answered, “Amen! Amen!” Then they bowed down and worshiped the LORD with their faces to the ground. Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodiah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan and Pelaiah, the Levites, helped the people understand the law, while the people stayed where they stood. They read from the book, from the law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood what was read.

Then Nehemiah, who was the governor, and Ezra the priest and scribe, and the Levites who were teaching the people said to all the people, “This day is holy to the LORD your God. Do not mourn and do not weep.” For all the people were weeping as they heard the words of the law. And he said to them, “Go, eat rich food and drink sweet drinks, and send portions to anyone who has nothing ready. For this day is holy to our Lord. Do not be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your stronghold.” The Levites calmed all the people, saying, “Be quiet, for this day is holy. Do not be grieved.” So all the people went away to eat and drink, to send portions, and to celebrate with great joy, because they had understood the words that had been made known to them.

Living in booths at the festival

On the second day the heads of the families of all the people, with the priests and the Levites, gathered around Ezra the scribe to study the words of the law more closely. And they found written in the law that the LORD had commanded through Moses that the Israelites were to live in booths during the festival of the seventh month, and that they should announce it and spread the word in all their towns and in Jerusalem: “Go out to the hills and bring branches of olive, wild olive, myrtle, palm and other leafy trees to make booths, as it is written.”

So the people went out and brought the branches and made booths for themselves, each on their own roof, in their courtyards, in the courtyards of the house of God, in the square by the Water Gate, and in the square by the Gate of Ephraim. The whole assembly of those who had come back from captivity made booths and lived in them. From the days of Joshua son of Nun until that day the Israelites had not done this. And there was very great joy. Day after day, from the first day to the last, Ezra read from the book of the law of God. They kept the festival for seven days, and on the eighth day there was a solemn assembly, as the law required.
fields.summary: Ezra reads the book of the law to the people, and the Levites explain it. The people weep, are told to rejoice, and live in booths during the festival of the seventh month.

fields.title: Nehemiah 9
fields.body_html:
A day of fasting and confession

On the twenty-fourth day of this month the Israelites gathered together, fasting, dressed in sackcloth, and with dust on their heads. Those of Israelite descent separated themselves from all foreigners. They stood and confessed their sins and the wrongs of their ancestors. They stood in their places and read from the book of the law of the LORD their God for a quarter of the day, and for another quarter they confessed their sins and worshiped the LORD their God.

The Levites lead the people in prayer

On the Levites’ platform stood Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani and Kenani, and they cried out with a loud voice to the LORD their God. Then the Levites Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabneiah, Sherebiah, Hodiah, Shebaniah and Pethahiah said, “Stand up and bless the LORD your God, from everlasting to everlasting! May your glorious name be blessed, which is exalted above all blessing and praise. You alone are the LORD. You made the heavens, the highest heavens and all their host, the earth and all that is on it, the seas and all that is in them. You give life to all of them, and the host of heaven worships you. You are the LORD, the God who chose Abram and brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans and gave him the name Abraham. You found his heart faithful before you, and you made a covenant with him to give the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites and the Girgashites, to give it to his descendants. And you have kept your word, for you are righteous. You saw the suffering of our ancestors in Egypt and heard their cry at the Red Sea. You performed signs and wonders against Pharaoh, against all his officials and against all the people of his land, for you knew how arrogantly they had treated our ancestors. And you made a name for yourself that remains to this day. You split the sea open before them, and they went through the middle of the sea on dry ground. But you hurled their pursuers into the depths, like a stone into mighty waters. By day you led them with a pillar of cloud, and by night with a pillar of fire, to light up the way for them in which they should go. You came down on Mount Sinai and spoke with them from heaven. You gave them right rulings and true laws, good statutes and commandments. You made known to them your holy Sabbath, and through Moses your servant you commanded them commandments, statutes and law. You gave them bread from heaven when they were hungry, and brought water out of the rock for them when they were thirsty. And you told them to go in and take possession of the land that you had sworn to give them. But they, our ancestors, acted arrogantly. They stiffened their necks and would not obey your commandments. They refused to listen and did not remember the wonders you had done among them. They stiffened their necks and in their rebellion appointed a leader to go back to their slavery. But you are a God who forgives, gracious and full of compassion, slow to become angry and rich in faithful love, and you did not abandon them. Even when they made for themselves a calf of cast metal and said, ‘This is your god who brought you up out of Egypt,’ and committed great blasphemies, you in your great compassion did not abandon them in the wilderness. The pillar of cloud did not leave them by day, to lead them on their way, nor the pillar of fire by night, to light up the way they should go. You gave your good Spirit to instruct them. You did not hold back your manna from their mouths, and you gave them water for their thirst. For forty years you provided for them in the wilderness, and they lacked nothing. Their clothes did not wear out, and their feet did not swell. You gave them kingdoms and peoples, and allotted them every region as their share. They took possession of the land of Sihon, the king of Heshbon, and the land of Og king of Bashan. You made their children as many as the stars of the sky, and you brought them into the land that you had told their ancestors to enter and possess. So the children went in and took possession of the land. You subdued before them the Canaanites who lived in the land and gave them into their hands, with their kings and the peoples of the land, to deal with them as they pleased. They captured fortified cities and fertile land and took possession of houses full of all good things, cisterns already dug, vineyards, olive groves and fruit trees in plenty. They ate and were filled and grew fat, and they delighted in your great goodness. But they were disobedient and rebelled against you. They threw your law behind their backs and killed your prophets, who had warned them in order to turn them back to you, and they committed great blasphemies. So you handed them over to their enemies, who oppressed them. But in the time of their distress they cried out to you, and you heard from heaven, and in your great compassion you gave them deliverers who rescued them from the power of their enemies. But as soon as they had rest, they again did evil in your sight, and you abandoned them to their enemies, who ruled over them. When they cried out to you again, you heard from heaven, and in your compassion you rescued them many times. You warned them in order to turn them back to your law, yet they acted arrogantly and would not obey your commandments. They sinned against your rulings, by which anyone who keeps them will live. They turned a stubborn shoulder, stiffened their necks and would not obey. For many years you were patient with them, and you warned them by your Spirit through your prophets. But they would not listen, so you gave them into the hand of the peoples of the lands. Yet in your great compassion you did not put an end to them or abandon them, for you are a gracious and compassionate God. So now, our God, the great, mighty and awesome God, who keeps covenant and faithful love, do not treat as small before you all the hardship that has come upon us, upon our kings, our officials, our priests, our prophets, our ancestors and all your people, from the days of the kings of Assyria until today. Yet you have been righteous in all that has come upon us; you have acted faithfully, while we have done wrong. Our kings, our officials, our priests and our ancestors did not keep your law or pay attention to your commandments and the decrees by which you warned them. Even in their own kingdom, with your great goodness that you gave them, and in the broad and fertile land you set before them, they did not serve you or turn from their evil deeds. See, we are slaves today, slaves in the very land you gave our ancestors so that they could eat its fruit and enjoy its good things. Its rich produce goes to the kings you have set over us because of our sins. They rule over our bodies and over our livestock as they please, and we are in great distress.”

Because of all this, we are making a binding agreement and putting it in writing. On the sealed document are the names of our officials, our Levites and our priests.
fields.summary: The people fast and confess their sins, and the Levites recount God’s faithfulness from creation through the exodus, the wilderness and the land, despite Israel’s rebellion.

fields.title: Nehemiah 10
fields.body_html:
The people seal a firm agreement

Those who sealed it were Nehemiah the governor, son of Hacaliah, and Zedekiah, Seraiah, Azariah, Jeremiah, Pashhur, Amariah, Malkijah, Hattush, Shebaniah, Malluch, Harim, Meremoth, Obadiah, Daniel, Ginnethon, Baruch, Meshullam, Abijah, Mijamin, Maaziah, Bilgai and Shemaiah. These were the priests.

The Levites: Jeshua son of Azaniah, Binnui of the descendants of Henadad, Kadmiel, and their fellow Levites: Shebaniah, Hodiah, Kelita, Pelaiah, Hanan, Mica, Rehob, Hashabiah, Zaccur, Sherebiah, Shebaniah, Hodiah, Bani and Beninu.

The leaders of the people: Parosh, Pahath-Moab, Elam, Zattu, Bani, Bunni, Azgad, Bebai, Adonijah, Bigvai, Adin, Ater, Hezekiah, Azzur, Hodiah, Hashum, Bezai, Hariph, Anathoth, Nebai, Magpiash, Meshullam, Hezir, Meshezabel, Zadok, Jaddua, Pelatiah, Hanan, Anaiah, Hoshea, Hananiah, Hasshub, Hallohesh, Pilha, Shobek, Rehum, Hashabnah, Maaseiah, Ahiah, Hanan, Anan, Malluch, Harim and Baanah. The rest of the people, the priests, the Levites, the gatekeepers, the singers, the temple servants, and all who had separated themselves from the peoples of the lands to keep the law of God, together with their wives, their sons and their daughters, all who were old enough to understand, join their fellow Israelites, their nobles, and bind themselves with a curse and an oath to walk in the law of God that was given through Moses the servant of God, and to keep and carry out all the commandments of the LORD our Lord, his rulings and his statutes. We will not give our daughters in marriage to the peoples of the land or take their daughters as wives for our sons. When the peoples of the land bring goods or any grain to sell on the Sabbath day, we will not buy from them on the Sabbath or on a holy day. Every seventh year we will leave the land unworked and cancel every debt. We also took on ourselves the obligation to give about 1/8 ounce of silver each year for the service of the house of our God, for the bread set out in rows, the regular grain offering and the regular burnt offering, the offerings for the Sabbaths, the new moons and the appointed feasts, the holy offerings, the sin offerings to make atonement for Israel, and all the work of the house of our God.

We, the priests, the Levites and the people, have cast lots for the wood offering, to decide which of our families is to bring wood to the house of our God at the set times each year, to burn on the altar of the LORD our God, as it is written in the law. We will also bring the firstfruits of our soil and the firstfruits of all the fruit of every tree to the house of the LORD each year. As it is written in the law, we will bring the firstborn of our sons and of our livestock, the firstborn of our herds and of our flocks, to the house of our God, to the priests who serve in the house of our God. We will bring to the priests, to the storerooms of the house of our God, the first of our dough, our contributions, the fruit of every tree, the new wine and the olive oil; and we will bring the tithe of our crops to the Levites, for it is the Levites who collect the tithes in all the towns where we farm. A priest descended from Aaron is to be with the Levites when they collect the tithes, and the Levites are to bring a tenth of the tithes up to the house of our God, to the storerooms of the treasury. For the Israelites and the Levites are to bring the contributions of grain, new wine and olive oil to the storerooms, where the vessels of the sanctuary are kept and where the priests who serve, the gatekeepers and the singers are. We will not neglect the house of our God.
fields.summary: The leaders, Levites and priests seal a written agreement, and the people pledge to keep the law, the Sabbath and the offerings for the house of God.

fields.title: Nehemiah 11
fields.body_html:
One of ten to live in Jerusalem, the holy city

The officials of the people settled in Jerusalem. The rest of the people cast lots to bring one out of every ten to live in Jerusalem, the holy city, while the other nine stayed in the other towns. The people blessed all the men who volunteered to live in Jerusalem.

The leaders who lived in Jerusalem

These are the leaders of the province who lived in Jerusalem. In the towns of Judah lived the Israelites, the priests, the Levites, the temple servants and the descendants of Solomon’s servants, every family on its own property in their towns. Some of the descendants of Judah and some of the descendants of Benjamin lived in Jerusalem. From the descendants of Judah: Athaiah son of Uzziah, son of Zechariah, son of Amariah, son of Shephatiah, son of Mahalalel, a descendant of Perez; and Maaseiah son of Baruch, son of Col-Hozeh, son of Hazaiah, son of Adaiah, son of Joiarib, son of Zechariah, a descendant of the Shilonite. All the descendants of Perez who lived in Jerusalem were 468 able men.

These are the descendants of Benjamin: Sallu son of Meshullam, son of Joed, son of Pedaiah, son of Kolaiah, son of Maaseiah, son of Ithiel, son of Jeshaiah; and after him Gabbai and Sallai: 928 in all. Joel son of Zikri was their overseer, and Judah son of Hassenuah was second in command over the city.

From the priests: Jedaiah son of Joiarib, Jakin, Seraiah son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam, son of Zadok, son of Meraioth, son of Ahitub, the chief officer of the house of God, and their fellow priests who did the work of the temple, 822 in all; and Adaiah son of Jeroham, son of Pelaliah, son of Amzi, son of Zechariah, son of Pashhur, son of Malkijah, and his fellow priests, heads of families, 242 in all; and Amashsai son of Azarel, son of Ahzai, son of Meshillemoth, son of Immer, and their fellow priests, capable men, 128 in all. Their overseer was Zabdiel son of Haggedolim.

From the Levites: Shemaiah son of Hasshub, son of Azrikam, son of Hashabiah, son of Bunni; and Shabbethai and Jozabad, leaders of the Levites, who were in charge of the outside work of the house of God; and Mattaniah son of Mica, son of Zabdi, son of Asaph, the leader who began the thanksgiving at prayer; Bakbukiah, second among his fellow Levites; and Abda son of Shammua, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun. All the Levites in the holy city were 284.

The rest of Israel in the towns of Judah and Benjamin

The gatekeepers: Akkub, Talmon and their fellow gatekeepers, who kept watch at the gates, 172 in all. The rest of the Israelites, priests and Levites were in all the towns of Judah, every family on its own inherited land. The temple servants lived on the Ophel, and Ziha and Gishpa were in charge of the temple servants.

The overseer of the Levites in Jerusalem was Uzzi son of Bani, son of Hashabiah, son of Mattaniah, son of Mica, one of the descendants of Asaph, the singers who were responsible for the service of the house of God. For there was a command from the king concerning them, and a fixed arrangement for the singers, providing what each day required. Pethahiah son of Meshezabel, a descendant of Zerah son of Judah, was the king’s agent in every matter concerning the people. As for the villages with their fields, some of the descendants of Judah lived in Kiriath-arba and its surrounding towns, in Dibon and its surrounding towns, in Jekabzeel and its villages, in Jeshua, Moladah, Beth-pelet, Hazar-shual, Beersheba and its surrounding towns, Ziklag, Meconah and its surrounding towns, En-rimmon, Zorah, Jarmuth, Zanoah, Adullam and their villages, Lachish and its fields, and Azekah and its surrounding towns. So they settled from Beersheba to the valley of Hinnom. The descendants of Benjamin lived from Geba onward, in Micmash, Aija, Bethel and its surrounding towns, Anathoth, Nob, Ananiah, Hazor, Ramah, Gittaim, Hadid, Zeboim, Neballat, Lod and Ono, and Ge-harashim. Some divisions of the Levites that had been in Judah were joined to Benjamin.
fields.summary: One family in ten is chosen by lot to live in Jerusalem. The leaders and those living in the city and the towns are listed.

fields.title: Nehemiah 12
fields.body_html:
Priests and Levites who came up with Zerubbabel and Jeshua

These are the priests and Levites who came up with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and with Jeshua: Seraiah, Jeremiah, Ezra, Amariah, Malluch, Hattush, Shecaniah, Rehum, Meremoth, Iddo, Ginnethoi, Abijah, Mijamin, Moadiah, Bilgah, Shemaiah, Joiarib, Jedaiah, Sallu, Amok, Hilkiah, and Jedaiah. These were the leaders of the priests and their relatives in the days of Jeshua.

The Levites, and the heads of families in later days

The Levites were Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel, Sherebiah, Judah, and Mattaniah, who with his brothers was in charge of the songs of thanksgiving. Bakbukiah and Unni, their fellow Levites, stood opposite them as they served. Jeshua was the father of Joiakim, Joiakim the father of Eliashib, Eliashib the father of Joiada, Joiada the father of Jonathan, and Jonathan the father of Jaddua. In the days of Joiakim, these priests were heads of their families: for Seraiah, Meraiah; for Jeremiah, Hananiah; for Ezra, Meshullam; for Amariah, Jehohanan; for Mellichu, Jonathan; for Shebaniah, Joseph; for Harim, Adna; for Meraioth, Helkai; for Iddo, Zechariah; for Ginnethon, Meshullam; for Abijah, Zikri; for Miniamin, ...; for Moadiah, Piltai; for Bilgah, Shammua; for Shemaiah, Jehonathan; and for Joiarib, Mattenai; for Jedaiah, Uzzi; for Sallai, Kallai; for Amok, Eber; for Hilkiah, Hashabiah; and for Jedaiah, Nethanel. In the days of Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan and Jaddua, the Levites were recorded by the heads of their fathers’ houses, and so were the priests, up to the reign of Darius the Persian.

The descendants of Levi, the heads of fathers’ houses, were recorded in the Book of the Chronicles, up to the days of Johanan son of Eliashib. The leaders of the Levites were Hashabiah, Sherebiah, and Jeshua son of Kadmiel. Their fellow Levites stood opposite them to praise and give thanks, one group answering the other, as David the man of God had commanded. Mattaniah, Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Meshullam, Talmon, and Akkub were gatekeepers who stood guard at the storerooms by the gates. These served in the days of Joiakim son of Jeshua son of Jozadak, and in the days of Nehemiah the governor and of Ezra the priest and scribe.

The dedication of the wall of Jerusalem

At the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, the Levites were sought out from all the places where they lived and brought to Jerusalem to celebrate the dedication with joy, with songs of thanksgiving, and with the music of cymbals, harps, and lyres. And the sons of the singers gathered, both from the district around Jerusalem and from the villages of the Netophathites, and from Beth-gilgal and from the fields of Geba and Azmaveth, because the singers had built villages for themselves around Jerusalem. The priests and the Levites purified themselves, and then they purified the people, the gates, and the wall. And I brought the officials of Judah up on top of the wall, and I appointed two great thanksgiving choirs to walk in procession. One went to the right on top of the wall, toward the Dung Gate. Behind them walked Hoshaiah and half of the officials of Judah, with Azariah, Ezra, Meshullam, Judah, Benjamin, Shemaiah, and Jeremiah,

and some of the priests with trumpets. Then came Zechariah son of Jonathan son of Shemaiah son of Mattaniah son of Micaiah son of Zaccur son of Asaph, and his brothers Shemaiah, Azarel, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethanel, Judah, and Hanani, with the musical instruments of David the man of God. Ezra the scribe walked in front of them. At the Fountain Gate they went straight up the steps of the City of David, where the wall goes up, above the house of David, and on to the Water Gate on the east. The second choir went the opposite way, and I followed it with half of the people, on top of the wall, past the Tower of the Ovens to the Broad Wall, and above the Ephraim Gate, past the Jeshanah Gate and the Fish Gate, the Tower of Hananel and the Tower of the Hundred, as far as the Sheep Gate. And they stopped at the Gate of the Guard. So the two choirs that gave thanks took their places in the house of God. So did I, with half of the officials, and the priests Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Micaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah, with trumpets, and Maaseiah, Shemaiah, Eleazar, Uzzi, Jehohanan, Malkijah, Elam, and Ezer. And the singers sang out loud, with Izrahiah as their leader. That day they offered great sacrifices and rejoiced, because God had given them great joy. The women and children rejoiced too, and the joy of Jerusalem could be heard far away. And on that day men were appointed over the chambers for the stores, for the contributions, for the firstfruits and for the tithes, to gather into them from the fields of the towns the portions required by the law for the priests and for the Levites; for Judah rejoiced over the priests and the Levites who stood to serve. They performed the service of their God and the service of purification, and so did the singers and the gatekeepers, as David and his son Solomon had commanded. For long ago, in the days of David and Asaph, there were leaders of the singers, and there were songs of praise and thanksgiving to God. In the days of Zerubbabel and in the days of Nehemiah, all Israel gave the singers and the gatekeepers their daily portions. They set apart what was due to the Levites, and the Levites set apart what was due to the descendants of Aaron.
fields.summary: The priests and Levites are listed. The wall of Jerusalem is dedicated with two great choirs and the sound of rejoicing.

fields.title: Nehemiah 13
fields.body_html:
No Ammonite or Moabite in the assembly of God

On that day the book of Moses was read aloud for the people to hear, and in it was found written that no Ammonite or Moabite should ever enter the assembly of God, because they had not met the Israelites with food and water, but had hired Balaam against them to curse them; yet our God turned the curse into a blessing. When the people heard the law, they separated from Israel all who were of mixed descent. Before this, Eliashib the priest, who had been put in charge of the storerooms of the house of our God and was related to Tobiah, had made a large chamber for him, where formerly they had put the grain offering, the frankincense, and the vessels, and the tithes of grain, new wine, and olive oil commanded for the Levites, the singers, and the gatekeepers, and the contributions for the priests. While all this was happening I was not in Jerusalem, for in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes king of Babylon I had gone to the king. After some time I asked the king for leave and came to Jerusalem. Then I learned of the evil Eliashib had done for Tobiah by giving him a room in the courts of the house of God. I was very displeased, and I threw all of Tobiah’s household goods out of the room. Then I gave orders, and they purified the rooms. I brought back into them the utensils of the house of God, with the grain offerings and the frankincense.

I also learned that the portions of the Levites had not been given, so that the Levites and the singers who did the work had fled, each to his own field. So I contended with the officials and said, “Why is the house of God forsaken?” And I gathered the Levites and singers and set them at their posts. Then all Judah brought the tithe of the grain, new wine, and olive oil into the storehouses. And I appointed as treasurers over the storehouses Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe, and Pedaiah of the Levites, and as their assistant Hanan son of Zaccur son of Mattaniah, for they were counted reliable. Their duty was to distribute to their brothers.

Remember me, my God, for this, and do not wipe out the faithful deeds I have done for the house of my God and for its services. In those days I saw people in Judah treading winepresses on the Sabbath, bringing in heaps of grain and loading them on donkeys, along with wine, grapes, figs, and every kind of load, and bringing them into Jerusalem on the Sabbath day. I warned them on the day they sold food. Men of Tyre who lived there were bringing in fish and all kinds of goods and selling them on the Sabbath to the people of Judah, in Jerusalem itself. Then I contended with the nobles of Judah and said to them, “What is this evil thing you are doing, profaning the Sabbath day? Did not your ancestors do the same, so that our God brought all this disaster on us and on this city? Yet you are adding to the wrath on Israel by profaning the Sabbath.”

Keeping the Sabbath holy

When the shadows fell on the gates of Jerusalem before the Sabbath, I ordered the doors to be shut and gave orders that they were not to be opened until after the Sabbath. I stationed some of my own men at the gates so that no load could be brought in on the Sabbath day. Once or twice the traders and sellers of all kinds of goods spent the night outside Jerusalem. But I warned them, “Why are you spending the night by the wall? If you do it again, I will use force against you.” From then on they did not come on the Sabbath.

Then I told the Levites to purify themselves and come and guard the gates, so as to keep the Sabbath day holy. Remember me, my God, for this also, and spare me according to the greatness of your faithful love.

Foreign wives and the covenant of the priesthood

In those days I also saw the Jews who had married women of Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab. Half of their children spoke the language of Ashdod, or the language of one people or another, and they did not know how to speak the language of Judah. And I contended with them and cursed them, and I struck some of their men and pulled out their hair. And I made them swear by God, “You will not give your daughters to their sons, nor take any of their daughters for your sons or for yourselves.” “Did not Solomon king of Israel sin on account of such women? Among the many nations there was no king like him, and he was loved by his God, and God made him king over all Israel; yet even he was made to sin by foreign wives. Shall we then listen to you and do all this great evil, acting unfaithfully against our God by marrying foreign wives?” And one of the sons of Joiada son of Eliashib the high priest was son-in-law to Sanballat the Horonite; so I drove him away from me. Remember them, my God, because they have defiled the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites. So I purified them of everything foreign, and I set out the duties of the priests and the Levites, each in his own task, and I provided for the wood offering at the appointed times, and for the firstfruits. Remember me, my God, for good.
fields.summary: Nehemiah returns to find Tobiah living in the temple, the Levites unpaid and the Sabbath broken. He drives out Tobiah, restores the offerings and the Sabbath, and rebukes those who married foreign women.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
So I purified them of everything foreign, and I set out the duties of the priests and the Levites, each in his own task, and I provided for the wood offering at the appointed times, and for the firstfruits. Remember me, my God, for good.

— Nehemiah 13:30–31

Nehemiah ends as it began, with a man praying. But the mood has changed. The book that opened with tears for a broken wall closes with a governor tidying up after his people’s broken promises, and asking God, one last time, to remember him. In time, if not in the order of our Bibles, these are the last events in the Old Testament’s history. Its history does not end in triumph. It ends with a prayer.

The question the book leaves with you

Nehemiah did everything a leader could do. He prayed and planned, built the wall in fifty-two days, defended it, made the rich give back what they had taken from the poor, gathered the people to hear God’s word, led them in confession, and had them sign a covenant to keep it. The city was dedicated with such joy that it “could be heard far away.” And within a few years the temple storeroom held Tobiah’s furniture, the Levites had gone back to their fields, the Sabbath was a market day, and the old marriages were being made again.

That is the question Nehemiah leaves with every reader: what does it take to change a people? Walls can keep enemies out. They cannot keep hearts in. Good laws, clear teaching and solemn promises are gifts of God, and the book honours all of them. But the last chapter shows, with painful honesty, that they are not enough by themselves. The people needed something done in them that no governor could do.

Nehemiah’s repeated prayer, “Remember me, my God”, points the same way. He does not ask to be remembered for his success, which he knows is fragile. He asks God to keep faith with him, and, in one of those prayers, to spare him “according to the greatness of your faithful love.” At the end, even Nehemiah rests on mercy.

Where the story goes next

The prophet Malachi, who spoke to much the same community, rebukes many of the same sins: neglected tithes, careless priests, broken marriages. And he looks forward to the day when the Lord himself will come to his temple. The prophets before him had already said what that coming would bring. Through Jeremiah the LORD promised a new covenant:

“I will set my instruction deep inside them and write it on their hearts. I will be their God, and they will be my people.”

— Jeremiah 31:33

Ezra read the law to the people from a wooden platform. The new covenant writes it within them. The New Testament says that this is what Christ came to do, by his death and by the gift of his Spirit.

And the city Nehemiah rebuilt pointed beyond itself. The letter to the Hebrews says that Abraham “was waiting for the city with firm foundations, a city planned and built by God,” and tells its readers: “There is no city here that remains for us; the city we are looking for is the one still to come.” At the end of the Bible, John sees that city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven. Nehemiah ordered his gates shut at nightfall to keep the city safe. Of the new Jerusalem it is said, “Its gates will never be shut in the daytime, and there will be no night there.”

Where to go from here

Nehemiah has long been a favourite of preachers on prayer, leadership and the joy of God’s word. Some of the best of that work is in this library. A few places to begin:

  • On Nehemiah’s prayers (Nehemiah 1–2). The chapter “Arrow Prayers and Long Fasts” in The Prayers Jesus Learned, an Ochorus Original, on the months of fasting in Susa and the moment of prayer before the king; and E. M. Bounds’s Prayer and Praying Men, whose chapter “Nehemiah, the Praying Builder” dwells on Nehemiah weeping, fasting and praying at the news from Jerusalem.
  • On the joy of the LORD (Nehemiah 8:10). Two sermons on the same verse: Alexander Maclaren’s The Joy of the Lord and A. B. Simpson’s The Joy of the Lord.
  • On faithful service. Hannah Whitall Smith’s Old Testament Types and Teachings, whose chapter “Nehemiah: Faithful Service” reads the rebuilding of the walls as a picture of the believer’s work for God; and her chapter on Ezra, “Ezra: Restoration from Backsliding”, which treats the two books together.
  • On Ezra, who stands beside Nehemiah. Bounds’s chapter “Ezra, the Praying Reformer”, in the same book, on Ezra’s prayer of confession (Ezra 9–10); and Maclaren’s sermon Heroic Faith (Ezra 8:22–23).
  • On the whole story of the return. The Big Story, an Ochorus Original, whose chapter “Coming Home” tells the story of Ezra 1, Nehemiah 8 and Esther 4 together.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Nehemiah in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this book.

And then go back to the square by the Water Gate, where the people stood from morning until noon to hear God’s word, and wept, and were told to stop weeping and go and feast. It is still the right word for anyone who hears the law and grieves:

And he said to them, “Go, eat rich food and drink sweet drinks, and send portions to anyone who has nothing ready. For this day is holy to our Lord. Do not be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your stronghold.”

— Nehemiah 8:10
